definition: Felicitous means strikingly well suited, with a glow of happy luck about the fit.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word felicitous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know felicitous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her felicitous nickname for the wobbling robot — 'Sir Stumbles' — stuck within the hour.
Suitable stops short of felicitous — a suitable phrase does its job without delighting anyone.
Inspired goes further than felicitous — an inspired choice feels like a small stroke of genius no one else could have found.

Apt means exactly to the point — an apt remark hits its target cleanly and stops there. Felicitous starts from that same accuracy and adds a glow of happy luck: a felicitous phrase feels not only right but delightfully unforced, as if the fit itself were good fortune.

Fitting means suitable in a plain, dutiful way — a fitting tribute meets the occasion's requirements and nothing more. Felicitous praise goes further: a felicitous choice does not merely meet the requirement, it lands with a spark of charm that makes the fit itself a pleasure.

Asked to caption the yearbook photo of the flooded gymnasium, Rosa wrote 'Swim Team Tryouts,' a felicitous two words that said everything the four-paragraph article beside it had struggled to say.
Felicitous is stronger than 'fitting' because it carries a spark of happy luck—the phrase or choice lands so well that it feels both perfectly suited and delightfully unforced.
Felicitous belongs to reviews, toasts, and essays — praise for a choice of words, a name, a pairing that lands perfectly.
For everyday praise, 'spot-on' or 'well chosen' is plainer; reach for felicitous when the fit itself deserves applause.

For two years the town argued about what to call its new ferry.
The shortlist was dutiful and dull: Harbor Star, The Crossing, Spirit of Commerce.
Each name was defensible, and nobody could love any of them.

Then a fourth-grader wrote in to suggest Stitch, because the ferry 'sews the two shores together like a needle going back and forth.' The committee checked the archives and found, to its delight, that the very first boat on the route in 1871 had carried mail for a tailor's guild.
The choice was felicitous in a way no committee could have engineered: exactly right for the boat's work, and touched with the kind of luck that makes a name feel destined.
